The maths behind every prediction, for those who want it. Five operations, repeated, turn a chart into a probability; matching colours link each equation to its picture.
A 3 × 3 filter slides over the chart image. Each output value (blue) is a weighted sum of the patch under it (green), plus a bias.
ReLU keeps the positive responses; a 2 × 2 max (green) halves the resolution. Three blocks deep, the chart is 128 maps of 26 × 26.
The last maps are flattened, passed through a dense layer and squashed into one probability (blue). The marked point is the chart from the Analysis Lab above.
Binary cross-entropy compares each probability with the realised label. The validation loss (green) decides which epoch is kept.

A new way to investigate financial markets. Other platforms give you tools to interpret prices. Convolve gives you the infrastructure to build AI that interprets them.
Chart patterns are simple by design. Markets may not be.

Head and shoulders, triangles, moving-average crosses: classic technical analysis reduces a chart to a few shapes a person can name and draw by hand. Tested rigorously, many of them show little reliable edge. That is usually read as proof that charts carry no information. It may only show that the vocabulary was too small.
Maybe the patterns aren't meaningless. Maybe our methods are too simple.

If structure exists, it is likely nonlinear: combinations of shape, scale and context that nobody would write down as a rule. Convolutional networks learn exactly that kind of visual feature from data, which makes them one way to test the idea. Not proof of it. A network can just as easily learn noise, so every result faces the same three checks.
Thresholds and settings are chosen on validation data, then locked before the test set is scored.
Try enough settings on the same history and one will look brilliant by chance. Only data the model never influenced counts.
Every result is set against buy-and-hold and a passive mix with the same exposure.

Testing an idea like this properly used to take a team: data pipelines, GPUs, model code and the discipline to evaluate honestly. The aim is to make that method mainstream, so that anyone curious enough can run the experiment, read the evidence and accept it when the answer is no.
From a price series to a tested probability.
A trading idea enters Convolve as a rule about the future and leaves as a measured model. First, the rule becomes data.
Every price window becomes an image.
The label is the objective the network trains toward; the Labeling Optimizer searches for a good one.
The network only ever sees the image on the left. The bars to the right of the dashed line are what decided its label.
What the network computes on one chart.
Every response below zero is set to zero. Without this bend, stacked layers would collapse into one linear function and could never express “this shape matters only next to that one”.

Each filter outputs a map of where its pattern occurred. Pooling halves the resolution after every block, so deeper maps see larger regions: early ones respond to wicks and edges, later ones to formations built from them.

This is the original Convolve CNN, one of seven networks in the Trainer. Each encodes a different assumption about where the signal sits: a dense head that keeps position or global pooling that discards it, residual depth, or ImageNet features reused by transfer. Optimiser, learning-rate schedule, dropout, L2 and augmentation are chosen per run as well. Trained on the same split, the variants are compared on validation and test data; a larger network is not presumed better.
One 3 × 3 filter on a real test chart, and the feature map it produces.
Learning is a descent on the loss.
Momentum overshoots, then settles. Plain descent creeps.
A model counts only on data it has never seen.
A later stretch of history is held out from fitting. It decides which epoch is kept and where the decision threshold sits, before any test result is looked at.

The locked model then trades the test period once, after costs, next to buy-and-hold and a passive mix with the same exposure. Classification accuracy and trading return are measured separately, because they can disagree. A strong backtest alone proves little: run enough variants over the same history and one will look excellent by chance.
Grad-CAM, saliency and occlusion show which pixels moved a prediction, so a learned price formation can be told apart from an artefact of how the chart was drawn.

What Convolve is and is not

Convolve is research software. It is not a bank, securities firm, broker, portfolio manager or financial adviser. It does not give personal recommendations, does not manage or hold your money or securities, has no connection to any brokerage account and does not execute real trades. Nothing on the website or in the workspace is an offer, solicitation or recommendation to buy or sell any financial instrument.

A paid subscription or credit pack buys access to software and computation for your own research. It is not a fee for advice, trading signals, model portfolios or the management of assets, and Convolve does not publish its own models, signals or strategies to subscribers.
This disclosure explains risks; it does not change the legal or regulatory obligations that may apply to you or to us.
A convolutional network learns statistical patterns in chart images. Those patterns may be noise, may not persist, and may fail suddenly when market conditions change.
A prediction is a probability produced by a model, not a statement about what will happen.
Interpretability tools such as Grad-CAM show where a model reacts in an image; they do not prove the model is right or that its reasoning is sound.
Past performance, real or simulated, does not guarantee future results.
Testing many label rules, thresholds or models on the same history increases the chance that a good result is luck (overfitting and data snooping).
Information leaking from the future into training or threshold selection can make results look better than they could have been.
Assumed commissions and slippage are simplifications. Real costs, spreads, liquidity, taxes and market impact can be higher and can turn a profitable backtest into a loss.

Historical data can contain errors, gaps, survivorship bias and adjustments. Convolve currently uses free, unlicensed data from Yahoo Finance (via yfinance), which is provided without any warranty of accuracy or availability.
Paper trades are simulated. No order reaches a market and no real position exists.
Simulated fills assume prices and quantities that may not have been available, and ignore partial fills, queue position, halts and outages.
Scheduled runs depend on data availability and infrastructure and can be delayed, skipped or paused.

What is stored in your browser

The website loads typefaces from Google Fonts; your browser therefore sends your IP address to Google. Google Fonts does not set cookies. If you choose to sign in with Google, Google sets its own cookies on its sign-in pages under Google's privacy policy.

When you buy a subscription or credits, or manage your billing, you are taken to our payment provider's checkout or billing pages. The provider sets its own cookies there, for example to prevent fraud and remember the payment session, under its own policy. Convolve's own pages still set no cookies.

You can delete local storage at any time in your browser settings. Signing out removes the session. If you clear storage you will be signed out and the workspace will forget local preferences; your research stored on our servers is not affected.
If we ever introduce optional analytics or similar technologies, we will ask for your consent first and let you change that choice at any time.
